slide_text: Inventing K-Means Clustering All the algorithms you've built so far have had labels — you knew the right answer and trained a model to predict it. But what if you just have a pile of data with no labels at all? Can you still find structure in it? You're about to find out — by grouping points that "belong together," using nothing but distances and averages. Navigate: press or Space to advance | to go back

Challenge (skip ahead if you can): Write that groups 2-D points into clusters. Pick starting centers, then repeat: assign each point to its nearest center, move each center to the mean of its points. Stop when the centers no longer move. Return the final centers and each point's cluster label. [code block] Test: [code block] Bonus: how would you choose when you don't know it? Try running with k = 1…6 and compare the total squared distance to the centers. Already got it? The next slides will guide you step by step.

Part 1: Grouping Points by Distance Here's a bunch of points scattered on a 2D plane. Your goal: split them into two groups so that points in the same group are close together. How would you start? You need some notion of a "center" for each group. The simplest idea: just pick two points and call them the centers. Then assign every point to whichever center is closer.

Distance Between Two Points Before you can group anything, you need to measure how far apart two points are. Write that returns a list of groups — one group per center. Each group is a list of points assigned to that center. Hint 1 Start with one empty list per center: . Loop through each point and compute its distance to every center. Hint 2 For each point, find which center gives the smallest distance, then append the point to that center's group. You can use .

Find New Centers You have two groups. The centers you started with were arbitrary — just the first two points. Now that you have groups, can you find better centers? What single point best represents a group of points? Write that returns a new list of centers — one per group. Hint 1 The "best representative" of a group of points is their average — the mean of all x-values and the mean of all y-values. Hint 2 For each group, sum all x-coordinates and divide by the number of points. Do the same for y-coordinates. Return the result as a new center: .

Quick Check — Grouping You assigned each point to its nearest center. If you moved one of the centers to a new location, what would happen? A. Nothing — once a point is assigned, it stays in that group forever B. Some points might now be closer to the other center, so their group assignment would change C. All points would switch to the other group D. The distances would not change because they depend only on the points, not the centers Answer: B. Distance depends on both the point and the center. Moving a center changes the distances, so some points may end up closer to a different center and switch groups.

See Your Clusters Run the plotting helper below to visualize the groups your algorithm found. The centers are shown as large X markers. Don't worry about understanding the plotting code — just run it and look at the result.

Congratulations! You just invented one of the most widely used algorithms in machine learning: K-Means clustering . Here's what you built: Your step The algorithm calls it Pick 2 starting points as centers Initialization Assign each point to the nearest center Assignment step Compute new centers as the group average Update step Repeat until centers stop moving Convergence K-Means is an unsupervised learning algorithm — it finds structure in data without any labels. No one told the algorithm which points belong together. It figured it out on its own, using nothing but distances and averages.

Quick Check — Why Does It Stop? In K-Means, you repeat: (1) assign points to nearest center, (2) move centers to the group average. Why does this process eventually stop changing? A. Python runs out of memory after too many loops B. The centers bounce back and forth forever — you just stop after a fixed number of steps C. Each step either keeps the total distance the same or makes it smaller, so the centers settle into a stable position D. The points physically move closer to the centers each round Answer: C. Every assign-then-update step reduces (or keeps equal) the total distance from points to their centers. Since it cannot keep getting smaller forever, the centers eventually settle and stop moving.

Quick Check — Going N-Dimensional Your original K-Means worked only in 2D. To make it work in 5D, which part(s) needed to change? A. Only the distance function — you loop over 5 coordinates instead of 2 B. Only the center computation — you average 5 coordinates instead of 2 C. Both the distance function and the center computation needed to loop over all dimensions D. The entire algorithm needs to be rewritten from scratch Answer: C. The assign-update loop itself stayed the same. Only the two helper functions (distance and center computation) needed to be generalized from 2 coordinates to N coordinates.

Part 4: How Many Groups? K-Means needs you to choose K — the number of groups. But how do you know the right K? What if you pick too many? Too few? Let's find out by measuring how "good" each grouping is.

Measuring Cluster Quality How tight are your clusters? One measure: for each point, compute its distance to its center. Sum up all these distances. A lower total means tighter clusters. Write that returns this total. Hint 1 For each group and its matching center, loop through every point in that group and add up . Hint 2 Use a nested loop: outer loop over , inner loop over points in each group. Keep a running total and return it at the end.
Try Different Values of K Run K-Means on the dataset below with k = 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6. Compute the inertia for each. What happens to the inertia as K increases?

The Elbow Method Plot inertia vs. K. The curve always goes down, but at some point the drop slows dramatically — like the bend of an elbow. That bend is your best K. Where is the elbow for the dataset above? Does it match the number of clusters we generated (3)?
Visualize Different K Values See what the clusters look like for different values of K. Run the code below to plot k=2, k=3, and k=5 side by side. Which one looks most natural?

Quick Check — Choosing K As you increase K (the number of clusters), what happens to the inertia (total distance from points to their centers)? A. It always goes up — more clusters means more total distance B. It always goes down — more clusters means each point is closer to a center — but the drop slows after a point C. It stays the same regardless of K D. It goes up and down randomly Answer: B. Adding more centers always makes (or keeps) the total distance smaller, because each point can find a center that is closer. But past the "right" number of clusters, the improvement becomes very small — that is the "elbow" you look for.

Part 6: Reflection

Reflection Answer these questions in your own words: What makes K-Means "unsupervised"? How is it different from the supervised algorithms you have seen (like decision trees or linear regression)? Why do the centers stop moving? Explain in your own words why the algorithm converges. What could go wrong with bad starting centers? If two initial centers land inside the same real cluster, what happens? Can you think of a way to choose better starting centers? Could K-Means group colors? If you represented colors as (R, G, B) triples with values 0-255, could you use K-Means to find the 5 "main" colors in a photograph? What would K be, and what would each dimension represent? When would K-Means fail? Imagine data arranged in two rings, one inside the other. Would K-Means with K=2 separate them correctly? Why or why not?
